title: Deterministic Validation with a Single‑Repair Guardrail for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We report a sealed, preregistered paired experiment that measured the marginal verifier-detected effect of interposing a deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair on the same LLM-generated configuration candidate. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial generation call per intent; that same candidate reused for both baseline and guarded episodes) we generated one candidate per natural-language intent with gpt-5-mini for N = 250 pairs and evaluated two episodes per intent: baseline (accept candidate) and guarded (deterministic validator; if failing, permit one automated repair). Execution completed 500 episodes with model_calls_used = 251. Results: baseline verifier-pass 249/250 (99.6%), guarded verifier-pass 250/250 (100.0%); contingency n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp] (paired bootstrap percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The single discordant pair was converted to pass by the single permitted repair. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the registered evidence bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored as intent-to-configuration translators in network operations (NetOps), offering the potential to convert operator natural-language intents into device CLI sequences. Stochastic generation, however, creates operational risks—syntax errors, command-ordering mistakes, and local-policy violations—that deterministic verification can detect before deployment. Architectures that place a validator between generation and acceptance, optionally followed by bounded automated repair (generate–verify–repair, GVR), are a standard defensive pattern for reducing mechanically checkable errors and for producing verifiable candidates before human or automated application [1]–[4].

This study quantifies the marginal verifier-detected benefit of inserting a deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair on an identical initial LLM candidate. Crucially, the experiment follows preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent we produced exactly one initial model generation and reused that same candidate for both the baseline and guarded episodes. This paired, shared-candidate design isolates only the deterministic validator + single-repair marginal effect on identical generated outputs, avoiding conflation with inter-run generation variability. We executed N_pairs = 250 constrained synthetic/emulation intents with declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic network validator that checks syntactic, ordering, and task-encoded final_state properties. We report concrete, artifact-grounded reconciliation and inference: baseline pass 249/250, guarded pass 250/250, paired difference 0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.
sections.related_work:
Prior empirical and survey work demonstrates that LLMs can produce usable draft network configurations under controlled conditions, while also emphasizing the role of verification and human oversight to catch residual mechanical and semantic errors [1], [2], [5]. Deterministic verification tools and formal-analysis techniques (e.g., Batfish-style analyses, header-space approaches, model checking) are mature components for checking forwarding, reachability, and many local-policy properties, and they serve as validators in GVR-style pipelines [6], [7]. Work on generate-and-validate or generate-and-repair in code and configuration domains shows improved detection and repair rates for mechanically verifiable defects, although semantic correctness beyond mechanically checkable properties remains challenging [3], [8].

Security analyses highlight prompt-injection and retrieval-based threats to LLM-integrated pipelines and motivate layered defenses (filtering, injection detectors, and conservative validators) for NetOps workflows [9]. Surveys from 2023–2026 also document heterogenous benchmarks and evaluation practices for LLMs in NetOps, underscoring the need for reproducible task banks, deterministic validators, and artifact-backed studies to measure marginal pipeline effects precisely [2], [5]. Our study differs by using a sealed preregistration with shared_initial_candidate semantics and by archiving deterministic reconciliation that proves provider-call accounting (shared initial generations = 250; repair calls = 1) and the exact paired contingency observed.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered a confirmatory paired design (study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1) with N_pairs = 250, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, and primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration froze the single-repair policy (at most one deterministic template-driven repair per episode), exclusion and contamination rules, and primary analysis (exact two‑sided McNemar plus paired-bootstrap percentile CI). The immutable preregistration artifact is archived in the evidence bundle.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and provider-call accounting. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one initial model generation call was produced per intent and that same candidate was evaluated in both baseline and guarded episodes; no independent per-condition first-pass generations were made. Provider-call reconciliation in archived manifests records hosted_model_call_event_count = 251, mapping to 250 shared_initial_generation calls and 1 repair-stage call. This deterministic reconciliation demonstrates the experiment measured the validator-and-single-repair marginal effect on identical candidates rather than effects of different initial generations across conditions.

Task generation and constraints. A deterministic task generator produced 250 constrained intents. Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and a difficulty label (medium/hard/very_hard). Tasks exercised common operational constraints (make-before-break uplink switchover, paired-link atomic MTU changes, safe access transfer patterns) and declared protected interfaces. All task payloads and the task manifest are archived.

Guarded pipeline, validator, and repair. The guarded pipeline submitted the shared candidate to a deterministic network validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) that parses CLI sequences, computes parsed_command_count, checks required_sequence ordering and workflow constraints, and materializes a final_state snapshot compared to the task's expected_final_state. The validator returns normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, and a boolean valid flag. When valid = false, the pipeline permitted a single automated repair attempt using constrained deterministic templates (reorder commands to match required_sequence; split/join command lines; correct evident token-ordering errors). Repairs were limited to syntactic and ordering fixes; no multi-iteration repair or human escalation was allowed. Repair templates, validator rules, and scoring logic are documented and archived in the evidence bundle.

Inclusion and contamination rules. Exclusion rules removed items failing deterministic vendor-parsers that prevented verification or items containing credential-like tokens or denylisted fragments. Contamination detectors flagged instruction-like embedded tokens or private-address artifacts. In the confirmatory run no episodes were excluded or flagged and complete_pair_count = 250.

Analysis and statistical inference. The preregistered primary analysis used a paired binary executor. We report the exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant counts and a paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) for the paired difference (guarded − baseline). All analysis inputs, code, and outputs are archived and deterministic reconciliation verifies the contingency counts used for inference.
sections.results:
Execution and counts. Execution completed the confirmatory partition with planned_episode_count = 500 and completed_episode_count = 500; model_calls_used = 251 reconciles to 250 shared initial-generation calls plus 1 repair call. No episodes were excluded; complete_pairs = 250.

Primary outcomes. Validator-scored successes: baseline_success_count = 249 (baseline_success_rate = 0.996), guarded_success_count = 250 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The observed paired contingency is n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The single discordant pair (baseline failed, guarded passed) corresponds to the only exercised automated repair; repair-conversion rate on the confirmatory partition = 1/250 = 0.004 (0.4%).

Statistical inference. The exact McNemar two-sided test on discordant counts (n10 = 1, n01 = 0) yields p = 1.0. The paired-bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval for guarded − baseline (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.012] (0 – 1.2 percentage points). These numeric outputs and the bootstrap parameters are present in the archived analysis artifacts.

Validator diagnostics and repair trace. Representative validator traces show parsed_command_count matching required_command_count for passed episodes; for example a medium-difficulty task had parsed_command_count = required_command_count = 4 and valid = true (representative traces archived). The sole repair trace converted a failing candidate to a pass per the constrained repair template; both the repair prompt/trace and the guarded scoring artifact for that pair are archived.
sections.discussion:
Empirical interpretation. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the constrained synthetic/emulation tasks used here, the marginal verifier-detected benefit of adding a deterministic validator plus a single automated repair was small: initial gpt-5-mini candidates satisfied the validator in 249/250 cases and the single permitted repair converted the only failing candidate. The paired-bootstrap CI upper bound (1.2 percentage points) bounds the maximum verifier-detected improvement under these pipeline and task conditions. This finding is a narrow, artifact-grounded quantification of the marginal verifier effect for identical initial candidates under constrained task semantics.

Why the observed gain is small. Artifact-grounded explanations include: (1) constrained task generation reduced intent ambiguity and limited allowed_touched_fields and required_sequence ambiguity, increasing the chance an LLM produces validator-conforming sequences; (2) the declared model (gpt-5-mini) produced consistent, syntactically well-formed sequences for these tasks; and (3) the deterministic validator measures mechanically verifiable properties (syntax, ordering, expected_final_state) and does not capture higher-order semantic correctness or dynamic protocol interactions that could be detected only by richer validators or live testing.

Power and preregistered assumptions. The preregistration used a power calculation that assumed baseline pass ≈ 0.90 and targeted detecting a 15 percentage-point absolute paired effect with N_pairs = 250 (≈80% power). The realized baseline pass rate (0.996) substantially exceeded the assumed value, reducing the experiment's power to detect small absolute improvements. Given this, the paired-bootstrap CI that bounds plausible verifier improvement under the study conditions is the most informative practical outcome rather than a hypothesis rejection.

Threats to validity and scope. Internal validity: results depend on the exact prompt templates, the single-repair policy, shared_initial_candidate semantics, and the validator's encoding. Construct validity: the deterministic validator checks mechanically verifiable properties but does not assert live protocol-level correctness or emergent multi-device behaviors. External validity: the confirmatory evidence covers only the deterministic synthetic/emulation partition; the preregistered community and production-like partitions were not executed in this run. Security: adaptive prompt-injection and retrieval-based adversaries were not exercised.

Operational implications. The small marginal verifier-detected gain observed here suggests that, in constrained emulation-style tasks with a capable LLM, a single automated repair may often be unnecessary for validator-class errors because initial candidates already satisfy mechanized checks. However, this result should not be generalized to adversarial, heterogeneous, or production contexts without additional evaluation: richer validators, multi-iteration repairs, human escalation, or live functional tests could detect and correct different error classes not exercised here. The study quantifies only the verifier-detected marginal impact on identical generated candidates under the confirmed execution contract.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure the deterministic-validator-plus-single-repair marginal impact on identical LLM-generated configuration candidates. In 250 constrained synthetic intents, initial gpt-5-mini candidates passed the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases; the guarded pipeline converted the sole failing candidate via the single permitted repair. Observed paired improvement = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp]; exact McNemar p = 1.0). The preregistered sim-to-real contrasts were not executed; results apply to the synthetic/emulation partition only. Broader evaluations (production-like topologies, adversarial injections, multi-model and multi-iteration repair strategies) remain necessary to assess generality. All execution and analysis manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

disclosure_statement:
Human role and autonomy boundary: After an autonomy lock required by the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track, the autonomous system performed literature search, study selection, preregistration freeze, prompt preservation, model calls, deterministic validation, permitted repair execution, analysis, drafting, peer-review, revision, and finalization without manual human editing of technical content. A human Research Director selected the broad topic family and performed pre-lock infrastructure development only; no human manually edited manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.

Models, tools, and framework: declared model = gpt-5-mini; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; deterministic task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution used a guarded generate–verify–repair flow permitting at most one automated repair per episode. Provider-call accounting reconciles to model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial_generation + 1 repair) with per-stage counts recorded in the archived reconciliation artifact.

Preregistration and immutable prompt reference: the study was preregistered under study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1 and the immutable master prompt used to initiate the autonomous run is archived as provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA-256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The evidence bundle contains the archived preregistration, execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts referenced in this manuscript.
limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production-like partitions were not executed and remain exploratory.

Deterministic validator assessed mechanically verifiable properties (syntax and prescribed workflow sequences) but did not measure broader semantic or behavioral correctness (protocol dynamics, emergent interactions).
Single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were used; results do not establish multi-model or alternate-validator generality.
Only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi-iteration repairs or human-in-the-loop escalation were not evaluated.
Adversarial and retrieval-based attacks (adaptive prompt-injection, vendor-targeted exploit vectors) and large-scale production heterogeneity were not exercised and remain open threats.
